course_details.Overview of class: How does music show up in our day-to-day lives? This course reflects on music as a historical, social, political and cultural phenomenon, permeating our lives far beyond entertainment. As we cover a myriad of genres from classical and jazz to film and popular music, students will develop an analytical tool kit that will allow them to think critically about music and its entanglements with the socio-cultural conditions that characterize its creation. The course is primarily designed around discussion and activity-based learning. Assessments will include weekly close reading and listening assignments, in-class activities and discussion, as well as a final creative project. Students will encounter the basics of music theory, however the ability to read music is not required to take this course.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): None required for purchase. All course material will be posted to CANVAS.

course_details.Overview of class: How does a piece of music become a classic, and who decides which music belongs in the canon at all? This course introduces students to concepts and vocabulary for listening to, talking about, and writing about music, using the idea of the canon as its guiding question. The first half of the quarter follows the conventional canon of Western art music, from Bach through Mozart and Beethoven to Stravinsky, while building skills in hearing and describing melody, rhythm, texture, and instrumentation. The second half turns to musicians whose work entered a canon of its own in the 20th and 21st centuries, including the North Indian classical (Hindustani) sitarist Ravi Shankar, the jazz saxophonist John Coltrane, and Kendrick Lamar, who in 2018 became the first rapper to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Moving between these two halves, students will consider how critics, prizes, and audiences shape musical reputations, and what each canon includes and leaves out. No previous musical training or ability to read music notation is required.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): None required for purchase. All readings and listening will be provided on CANVAS.

course_details.Overview of class: This course examines how music impacts and reflects our everyday lives, particularly in the way it shapes our selfhood, our relationships to our communities, and Western culture at large. Covering myriad genres from classical to pop, students will develop fundamental technical language to analyze what they are hearing, and will explore and critique the sociocultural conditions that surround musical creation. The course is primarily designed around discussion- and activity-based learning. Assessments include weekly reading and listening, participation in in-class and online discussions, and three mini "deep-dive" projects. The ability to read music is not required to take this course.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): None required for purchase. Assigned reading, listening, and other materials will be available on CANVAS or on YouTube.

course_details.Overview of class: Chamber music refers to music written for small groups of players, to be performed in a royal court, private home, or (later) public recital hall. Over the course of its history - from the 16th century to the present - chamber music has served as an important locus of musical innovation, from Monteverdi's madrigals to the string quartets of Haydn, Beethoven and Shostakovich. Our course will explore this broad category of musicking from the perspective of its composers, performers, distinctive styles and genres, as well as its relation to certain categories of experience such as: class, politics, religion, gender, and the family. We will take an expansive view of the term "chamber music," allowing us to explore additional musical forms outside of the strictly Western classical tradition. In-class learning is discussion based, with the expectation of weekly reading and listening outside of class time. Assessments will include in-class participation as well as reading quizzes, listening reflections, and two in-class exams. The ability to read music is not required.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): None required for purchase. All materials will be made available through CANVAS.

course_details.Overview of class: Opera and Gender will first introduce students to opera - its characteristics, history, and development over time - and then invite them to engage with the intersection of this artistic form with considerations of gender. Our four main perspectives of inquiry will be: music, narrative, vocalism, and people - audience members, performers, and composers of opera. Students will be able to identify, analyze, and describe ways in which gender impacts and influences elements such as musical material, plot, production, characterization, staging, dramaturgy, and social/cultural context with regards to the operatic form. For the purposes of this course, we will utilize a broad definition of "opera" and examine a wide range of material, comparing how gendered factors function in a variety of compositions, contexts, and time periods, addressing topics from castrati to travesti, works from Antonín Dvořák's The Devil and Kate to Kate Soper's Here Be Sirens, and composers from Francesca Caccini to Sarah Kirkland Snider. Class time will be used for a mix of lecture, listening/watching, analysis, discussion, and active learning, and assignments will mainly consist of reading, listening/watching, and written responses. Because this course will serve as an introduction to the concept of opera as a whole, as well as its relationship to gender, no previous musical experience is necessary.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): None required for purchase. All materials and readings will be provided by the instructor.

course_details.Overview of class: How does music intersect with politics and shape political thinking? This course offers a survey of music's involvement in political life, from the sixteenth century to the current day. Content will be drawn from diverse times, genres, and geographies, with special attention given to dimensions of agency and power.
course_details.Learning Objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to identify, compare, and offer critical perspectives on musical works from a wide array of cultural and political contexts. Through comparative analyses and inquiry-based learning, students will become adept at recognizing the historical, political, and musical factors which determine how political messages are artistically created and received. Students will be able to critically listen to music, recognizing how their own historical-political contexts shape the way in which they think about music as politicized or depoliticized.
course_details.Teaching Method: Course meetings will be divided into lecture and active learning components, with the exception of exam days. Active learning components are frequently discussion-based and collaborative, involving presentation of the student's idea to a peer or the entire class.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Students will be evaluated through attendance and participation, four unit assessments, and a final oral exam. All components are weighted equally. All assessment types will have listening components and open-ended questions relating to musical material and ideas from class. For oral exams, students will be tested on musical examples of their choosing in accordance with the instructor's requirements. Final oral exams will be conducted in person.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): None required for purchase. All reading materials will be provided on CANVAS.
course_details.Class Materials (Suggested): Notebook and writing utensils. Electronics are not permitted, unless required by an active learning activity.

course_details.Overview of class:
Food and music are two of the most universal features of human experience, shaping identity, memory, ritual, and social connection around the world. Their intersection raises fascinating questions: Can music change the way food tastes? Why do particular foods and sounds become meaningful to different cultures and communities? How have food and music worked together throughout history to shape daily life?

This course explores the connections between food and music from psychological, social, cultural, and historical perspectives. Through readings, class activities and discussions, and individual projects, students will examine theories of cross-model perception and multisensory experience while considering the personal and cultural meanings we attach to different kinds of foods and sounds. Topics will include restaurant and grocery store atmospherics, music in food production, ceremonies and celebrations, food imagery in lyrics and music videos, marketing and branding, and more. By the end of the course, students will have explored a wide range of topics at the intersection of food and music and developed new ways to critically examine food-music pairings they encounter in everyday life.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): None required for purchase. All course material will be posted to CANVAS.

course_details.Overview of class: This course is intended to provide students with analytical tools to understand how pop songs work. We will reflect on the conditions that define pop music, expanding this conception with examples of songs and albums from the last 10 years that push or subvert these conditions. We will draw examples from well-known artists like Tinashe, Solange, and Caroline Polachek, as well as lesser-known artists like Marina Herlop and Fuensanta, studying these examples along with their musical influences and cultural meaning. Previous music theory knowledge is not required. We will develop a listening strategy to describe how the music works by answering concrete questions about the characteristics of the songs analyzed. Students will be evaluated through a series of reading and listening responses.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): None required for purchase. All course material will be posted to CANVAS.
